title: Coding sessions
text: Docs Sign up Open app Getting started Intake Projects and initiatives Issues and cycles Coding and review Coding sessions Reviews Releases Coding settings Agents and automation Linear Agent Loops AI Agents Assign and delegate issues Triage Intelligence Code Intelligence Coding sessions MCP server Insights and outcomes Working in Linear Integrations Administration Importers Docs Developers Learn Contact support Coding and review Coding sessions Copy page Sign up Open app Coding sessions Overview ⁠ Coding sessions let Linear Agent work on your issues using Claude Code or Codex. Delegate a well-scoped issue, and Linear Agent writes and tests the change in a secure cloud environment, then returns a draft pull request for review. Teammates with repository access can follow progress, add context, steer the approach, and review the diff in Linear. Existing GitHub permissions and review requirements still determine what ships. Use coding sessions to: Fix bugs from your backlog or Triage Make contained changes with clear outcomes and constraints Address review comments, rebase branches, fix lint issues, or add tests Delegate smaller changes without setting up a local environment Coding sessions are supported on paid plans. Usage draws from your workspace’s AI credits. See AI credits for more information. To review coding session spending and manage spend limits, open Settings → Usage & limits . Learn more about usage and spend limits . Setup ⁠ A Linear owner or admin with GitHub organization owner access can enable coding sessions within your workspace by: Navigating into your GitHub Integration settings and granting code access Enabling Coding sessions If your GitHub organization or services accessed by coding sessions use IP allow lists, allow the Coding sessions IPs listed under GitHub Enterprise Cloud in the GitHub integration documentation . Afterwards, any workspace member with a GitHub account linked in Connected Accounts will be able to start a coding session. Choose a model ⁠ Our current default model (tracked under Auto ) is GPT-6 Sol. The model selected here is used for all subsequent coding sessions in the workspace. Workspace owners or admins can update the model selection from Coding sessions settings . We currently support Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 5; GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.4; and GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash. Configure coding environments ⁠ Coding environments let workspace owners and admins configure repository-specific setup for coding sessions. Use them to provide the runtimes, tools, configuration, and instructions the agent needs to work in a particular codebase. To create an environment, go to Workspace settings → AI & Agents → Coding sessions → Environments . Configure an environment ⁠ You can configure: Runtimes and tools: Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, PostgreSQL, and Redis, including specific runtime versions. Environment variables: Use these for required runtime configuration. Names and values are visible to the coding agent and should not be treated as agent-hidden secrets. Prepare script: Run setup commands during environment preparation. Files: Add text files at relative paths in the environment home directory, such as .npmrc. Custom guidance: Provide repository-specific instructions for how the agent should work. Agent and model: Choose an agent and model for the environment. Available options depend on the selected model and workspace configuration. Environment secrets ⁠ Coding environments can securely store credentials for private registries and authenticated services outside your repository. This gives agents access to the private dependencies and services they need to build and test your code. When creating a new environment variable for your environment, check the Secret checkbox to denote this state: Environment secrets are not visible to the coding agent by default, but are visible to anyone who can run a session in that environment. Treat them as development-time secrets, like a local .env file, not as values hidden from your team. Limitations ⁠ An environment contains one repository, and a repository can belong to only one active environment. Repositories must be available through your workspace’s GitHub integration. Archived environments cannot be used for new coding sessions. Start a coding session ⁠ When you delegate work to Linear, Linear Agent creates an secure coding session tied to that issue and begins working from the context already there. Click on the session to steer or follow up with the agent, or let it run autonomously—you’ll be notified when your input is needed. When you ask Linear to make a change, Linear Agent starts working right away. That includes direct requests like fixing a bug, implementing a feature, opening a PR, or starting a coding session. If Linear has already offered to handle something, a quick reply like “proceed” is typically enough to begin. If you’re asking Linear to look into something first, it won’t start coding yet. Requests to investigate, debug, research, plan, or create the actual task are treated as scoping the problem, not implementing it. The same goes for messages that only say where the work should be tracked, like a team, project, cycle, milestone, or triage. As part of a coding session, Linear Agent can prepare projects that use supported runtimes, including Python, Ruby, Go, Rust, Java, and Node.js, and install dependencies from repository configuration and lockfiles. It can also start local applications, use browser automation to test changes, and capture screenshots or recordings for verification. Review code changes ⁠ When a coding session produces a pull request, the workflow continues in your Reviews tab, where you can inspect the resulting diffs and follow review discussions. When a session includes verification artifacts, you can review the screenshots or recordings alongside the proposed changes. You can also delegate code review actions to the Linear Agent directly to address any left review comments from other teammates, requirements to rebase open PRs onto master, or fixing tedious lint issues. Guidance and skills ⁠ Coding sessions work from the issue you delegate and the repository access available to your workspace, and the guidance configured for Linear Agent. Coding sessions are guided from the existing Claude Code or Codex setup your team already uses, depending on your preferred model. If your repositories include guidance within a dedicated skills.md file or supported tool-version configuration, Linear Agent can use that context alongside the issue and repository context during a coding session. Writing effective issues ⁠ Coding sessions begin from the issue you delegate. The more clearly an issue defines the desired outcome, scope, and constraints, the less time Linear spends exploring the codebase or inferring requirements. Too ambiguous Search is broken. Improve the search experience. Users can’t find archived projects through search. This should respect the Include archived toggle. Well-scoped Issue search excludes issues from archived projects, even when Include archived is enabled. Update issueSearch.ts so issue search respects the existing includeArchivedProjects flag. When enabled, issue search should include issues from archived projects that match the search query. When disabled, existing behavior should remain unchanged. Reuse the existing includeArchivedProjects filtering behavior used elsewhere in search rather than implementing archived project filtering independently. Do not modify search ranking, pagination, or project search behavior. The well-scoped example above points Linear toward the relevant code, existing patterns, and expected behavior while defining what should not change. Code Intelligence can also be a useful tool to help iterate on issue descriptions for optimization prior to delegation. Information that reduces ambiguity or codebase exploration helps Linear reach an implementation faster and use AI credits more efficiently. For more information about AI credits, see AI credits . Agent automations ⁠ Once you’ve enabled coding sessions, the next way to drive efficiency is to kick them off automatically. Triage automations let you run agent behaviors, including coding sessions, each time an issue arrives in Triage. Optionally, filter to run only when an issue meets specific criteria, like a label, creator, or other filterable property. Internally, our favorite way to use these automations has been to have Linear take the first pass at issues coming into Triage. Each time Triage Intelligence identifies a new issue in triage issue as a bug, this automation runs to investigate and draft a PR if called for. You can set up automations of your own in a team’s triage settings. AI credits ⁠ Coding sessions usage will draw from your workspace’s AI usage credits. Any chat or automation that prompts for a code change will open a coding session. Once used, workspace admins can top up AI credits to continue using coding sessions. Please see AI credits for more information. title: Smoothly transition from Jira to Linear
text: Integrations Jira Smoothly transition from Jira to Linear Automatically sync issues between Jira and Linear Automatically sync issues between Jira and Linear Jira issues are bi-directionally linked to Linear issues Overview ⁠ If you want to switch from Jira to Linear, this integration makes the process smoother by keeping projects up to date in Jira as you use Linear. How it works ⁠ This integration keeps Jira up to date while your company trials or transitions to Linear. First, you’ll connect specific Jira projects to Linear teams. New issues created in either service will create a synced copy in the other, with properties that sync bidirectionally. A synced comment thread in Linear will allow users to communicate back to the comment thread in Jira. For further details on the integration, please see our documentation . Once you’re ready to make the switch, use Linear’s quick Jira importer to move over all your existing issues in a few minutes. Configure ⁠ A Linear admin can go to settings to enable this integration, then link Jira projects to their corresponding teams in Linear. Configuration also requires ADMINISTER permission in Jira so that Linear can install the required webhooks. This integration is designed to work with newly created issues. For existing tickets, import those to Linear in a few minutes using our Issue Migration Assistant. title: Notifications
text: Docs Sign up Open app Getting started Intake Projects and initiatives Issues and cycles Coding and review Agents and automation Insights and outcomes Working in Linear Inbox My issues Pulse Favorites Notifications Preferences Profile Documents Board layout Timeline Custom Views Editor Search Filters Display options Security & Access Peek preview Integrations Administration Importers Docs Developers Learn Contact support Working in Linear Notifications Copy page Sign up Open app Notifications Receive alerts on important updates in the Linear desktop app, mobile app, Slack, or email. Overview ⁠ You’ll always see notifications in your Linear inbox. For real-time alerts, you can use the Linear desktop app, mobile app, Slack, or email digests. Configure ⁠ Go to Settings > Account > Notifications to manage your notifications. You can customize the types of updates you’d like to receive from Linear, such as changelogs, DPA updates and other communications. Notifications are categorized by channel: Desktop, Mobile, Email, and Slack. A green dot next to a channel means that notification method is enabled, while a gray dot means it is disabled. To enable a notification, select the notification method you’d like to configure and click the toggle to turn on the notification. You can then enable or disable each notification type. Notifications are grouped. For example, the status-changes category includes issue completions and cancelations, urgent-priority changes, and changes to blocking relationships. You cannot select only status changes. Notification timing ⁠ Desktop, mobile and Slack notifications are sent in real-time. Email digests send with time delays based on urgency, and are only sent if you haven’t already read the Linear inbox notification. Email notifications ⁠ There are two settings you can have for email notifications - email digest or immediate delivery. You can select your preferred frequency by clicking on the dropdown arrow in the Notification format selector. Email digests provide a summary of unread notifications. They’re configured to send out after a certain amount of time has elapsed depending on properties such as issue status. By default, notifications are grouped into digests and sent based on urgency. Email notification Subscribing to an issue ⁠ Subscribing to an issue determines whether notifications are received for that issue, based on notification preferences. You are automatically subscribed to an issue when you create it, are assigned to it, are @mentioned in an issue comment or description, or if you use the menu in the Activity section to subscribe manually. If you are @mentioned in a comment in an issue thread, you will be automatically subscribed to the thread, but not to the overall issue. To manage subscriptions, open issues individually and then press Shift S to subscribe or Cmd/Ctrl Shift S to unsubscribe. View all subscribed issues under My Issues > Subscribed . FAQ ⁠ My notifications are enabled. Why am I not receiving them? Notification delivery may be routed to an active desktop app or browser session. If none of those apply, please reach out to our support team. Do you support browser-based notifications? For real-time desktop notifications, use the Linear desktop app. Linear does not currently support setting up new browser push-notification subscriptions. You can still access all notifications in your Linear inbox, and use mobile, Slack, or email notifications based on your preferences. Why isn't the red badge showing up on the Linear icon in my dock? Please check that you’ve enabled notifications for Linear in the macOS settings as well as marked to show the red badge icon. What status changes generate notifications? When “Status changes” is selected in Notification settings, issue completions and cancelations will notify you if you subscribe to the issue. If you wish to configure notifications for issues entering a specific status, consider setting up a view subscription . Is there a limit to how many notifications you can keep in your inbox? Linear retains up to 2,000 open notifications in your inbox. When this limit is exceeded, notifications are automatically archived. title: Discord
text: Docs Sign up Open app Getting started Intake Projects and initiatives Issues and cycles Coding and review Agents and automation Insights and outcomes Working in Linear Integrations Integration Directory MCP server Airbyte Linear Asks Discord Figma Front GitHub GitLab Google Sheets Gong Intercom Jira Microsoft Teams Notion Salesforce Sentry Slack Zapier Zendesk Administration Importers Docs Developers Learn Contact support Integrations Discord Copy page Sign up Open app Discord Combine Linear with Discord to keep everyone in sync. Overview ⁠ Create issues and search for them from the Discord app. The wrap command will post a summary of your day’s work in the channel. Discord /linear issue to create an issue in Linear /linea r search to search and then post an issue /linear wrap to share a summary of your issue updates in the last 24 hours Configure ⁠ Connect to your Discord server to create issues from Discord messages, search issues, and use the wrap command. Integration setup ⁠ A Linear admin must first enable the integration for the workspace. Once they have, you can go to Settings > Integrations > Discord to connect your Discord account to Linear. Every Linear user must individually link their account in order to use the Linear integration in Discord. Once connected, anyone with a Linear account will be able to do the following: Create Linear issues from Discord with the /linear issue command. Search and display Linear issues in Discord Post a wrap, a summary of your days work, in your Discord channel. Basics ⁠ Create issues ⁠ Type the /linear issue command into any channel to create a Linear issue. You will need to fill in the issue title and team and you will also have the option to add a description, status, assignee and project. Search issues ⁠ Type the /linear search command into any channel to search Linear issues on your workspace. The application uses the same search as the app, so you can search for issues by issue ID or words in the title, description, or comments. Once you select the relevant issue and click enter, this will be posted to the channel for all members to see. Post your daily wrap ⁠ Type the /linear wrap command into any channel and click enter to post a summary of any issues you started or completed in the past day. Link Discord messages in Linear issues ⁠ Mouse Command menu Click on contextual menu icon … to the top right of the issue Click Add link Click Discord message discord when in issue view, then select Link Discord message… Unlink issues ⁠ You can remove a Discord link from the Linear issue by right-clicking on the issue attachment. Filter for Discord links ⁠ From any Linear view, you can filter by issues linked to Discord messages. Click F then select Links and then select Discord . FAQ ⁠ Why does the Discord integration need the "Read Message History" permission? We need it in order to fetch individual message data when linking a Discord message to an issue with the “Link Discord message” action. Will you support project update notifications for Discord? It’s something we’d like to support in the future, but no timeline on if/when that might be yet. If you’d like to see it, let us know at support@linear.app as we track demand. title: Project labels
text: Docs Sign up Open app Getting started Intake Projects and initiatives Projects Project milestones Project priority Project status Project labels Project dependencies Project notifications Project templates Initiatives Sub-initiatives Initiative and project updates Issues and cycles Coding and review Agents and automation Insights and outcomes Working in Linear Integrations Administration Importers Docs Developers Learn Contact support Projects and initiatives Project labels Copy page Sign up Open app Project labels Organize projects with custom labels relevant to your organization’s specific context. Filter projects or issues by their project’s label to clearly segment work. Workspace-level project labels are available on all plans. Creating team-level project labels requires a Business or Enterprise plan. Overview ⁠ Project labels categorize work at scale and make it easier to filter, group, and locate projects across your workspace. While Initiatives are a great way to group projects by overarching company goal, project labels provide a more flexible and granular grouping dimension. Use project labels to group project views and filter issues by the labels on their projects. This helps you see work contributing to a common area. Create a project label or group ⁠ In addition to workspace-level project labels, teams on Business and Enterprise plans can create team-level project labels. A team’s project labels are available on projects that include that team. Manage workspace-level project labels in Settings > Projects > Labels. Manage team-level project labels from the team’s settings. You can also create a project label from the label menu on a project. As with issue label groups, project label groups are mutually exclusive; only one sub-label per group may be applied to a project. Using labels across teams ⁠ When a project includes multiple teams, labels from each contributing team or its parent teams can be applied alongside workspace-level labels. If contributing teams have ungrouped labels with the same name, Linear presents them as one label in the picker and on the project. Labels in different groups, including child labels with the same name, remain separate labels. Removing teams from projects ⁠ Removing a team from a project also removes that team’s project labels from the project. A matching label from another contributing team remains applied when available. Privacy ⁠ Team-level project labels follow team visibility. Labels from private teams are only visible to people who can access those teams. Filtering and grouping ⁠ Filtering projects by their label or label group allows you to organize work in units that make sense for your business and the way your work gets done. Group projects by label or label group in project views, or issues by their project’s label in issue views. List project label columns ⁠ In a project list view, open Display and select a label group to show it as a column. Adding a project label column Insights ⁠ In Insights for an issue view, use project labels to break down issue count, issue age, or triage time by the labels on each issue’s project. Use this functionality to identify which upstream projects are driving the most work across your teams and compare performance metrics between project labels. title: Insights
text: Docs Sign up Open app Getting started Intake Projects and initiatives Issues and cycles Coding and review Agents and automation Insights and outcomes Dashboards Insights Project graph Cycle graph Working in Linear Integrations Administration Importers Docs Developers Learn Contact support Insights and outcomes Insights Copy page Sign up Open app Insights Real-time analytics for all your Linear data. Visualize issue data to spot trends and remove blockers. Available to workspaces on the Business and Enterprise plans. Overview ⁠ Insights turns your Linear issues into a dataset you can analyze to better understand how you work. Use Insights to answer questions like: What projects take up the most resources? How quickly do you fix bugs? How consistently do you prioritize issues? Do you estimate accurately? Configure ⁠ Most issue views in Linear have an Insights panel in the righthand sidebar, which you can open with Cmd/Ctrl Shift I . Find Insights in Custom Views as well as team, project, and cycle views. The best place to use Insights is in custom Views that are shared at the Workspace level. They offer the most flexibility and power, since you can access issue data from all teams and filter across any property (e.g. Label, Assignee, Project) in your workspace. Examples ⁠ The best way to learn how Insights works is to try it. We’ve built an in-app Help Center that walks you through common use cases. You can view instructions on how to create these examples or select a button to apply the example to your current view. Access the Help Center by selecting the … icon from the Insights panel and selecting Insights examples Create Insights ⁠ Apply filters ⁠ Insights will offer analytics for all the issues in the view you’re currently looking at. Add or remove filters to change which issues are included in the dataset. The following filters can be especially helpful when creating Insights. Filter Why it's helpful for Insights Created at Limits issues to those created during a certain timeframe Completed at Limits issues to those completed within a certain timeframe Status Type Works across teams (even if Statuses are named differently) Label, Project, Team Refines large views to most relevant issues To include Archived issues in your Insights analysis, open the Insights options (to the left of the three dot menu, just above the Segment dropdown) and toggle on Show archived issues . From there you can also filter out issues without a priority assignment. Select Insights Parameters ⁠ From the dropdown, choose the Measure and Slice for your Insight. This will generate a graph and table showing the data, with the Measure along the y-axis and Slice along the x-axis. Segments are optional and use color to slice the data further. Values for Measure , Slice , and Segment vary depending on what issues are displayed in your view. Measure What is it? Type of graph Automatic filters Issue count Total number of issues Bar None Effort Total estimate value Bar None Cycle Time Time from issue start to completion Scatterplot Only plots issues that spent time in progress before being completed Lead Time Time from issue creation to completion Scatterplot Only plots completed issues Triage Time Time issue spent in Triage status Scatterplot Only plots Triaged issues Issue Age Time since issue creation Scatterplot None Graph Interactions ⁠ Insight graphs are interactive, so that you can play with the dataset to learn more or focus on a specific type of issue. Bar graph ⁠ Hover over each bar to see data and percentile breakdowns. Select full bars or segments to temporarily filter your view to only those issues. Hovering or selecting bars or segments will highlight related data in the table below the graph. Scatterplot ⁠ Hover over the graph to see markers indicating that the data below the line represents 25%, 50%, 75%, and 95% of issues plotted. Select percentile markers to zoom in or out along the y-axis. Hover over points to see the issue details including the issue name, ID, and slice and segment values. This will also highlight related data in the table below the graph. Select points to go to open the related issue. Burn-up charts ⁠ Burn-up charts, or cumulative flow diagrams show how streams of work have changed over time. Unlike other insights, burn-up charts display your historical issue data so you can analyze and detect patterns across specific time windows. By default, burn-up charts show data in monthly increments. Adjust insights settings to plot the data week over week, or to include archived issues. When applicable, select Burn-up under the Slice menu to visualize your data in this style. Table (below graph) ⁠ Hover over row or specific cell to see corresponding data in graph Select row, column, or cell to temporarily filter issue view to only those issues Share Insights ⁠ Select the three dot menu on the top right of the Insights panel to share your Insight. Copy a link, which can be viewed by anyone else in your workspace Export to CSV, to explore the data outside of Linear Full Screen view ⁠ Insights can be opened in Full Screen view by selecting the expand button (just above the Segment dropdown). This gives you more room to explore the graph and table data. title: Connect v0 and Linear through MCP
text: Integrations v0 by Vercel MCP connector Connect v0 and Linear through MCP Overview ⁠ Connect the Linear MCP server to v0 so that you can pull issues, projects, and specs directly from Linear into v0 and start building. No more copy-pasting issues or switching between tabs - your Linear workspace becomes part of your development workflow in v0. How it works ⁠ v0 is an AI agent that helps anyone create real code and full-stack apps. Ship features, refine designs, update copy, and create live prototypes — all with a prompt. Deploy to production immediately, or open a pull request for review. The integration connects your issue tracking directly to your development environment in v0. Pull any Linear issue, project brief, or feature spec into v0 and use it as context while you build. Whether you’re working on a bug fix, new feature, or technical task, you can reference the original Linear issue without leaving v0. Once you’ve pulled an issue into v0, you can build the feature, iterate on it, and push to production. This integration is built for teams that live in Linear and want to close the gap between issue tracking and shipping code. Instead of managing context in multiple tools, you can go from Linear issue to deployed feature in one workflow. Your specs, bug reports, and feature requests become immediately actionable. Configure ⁠ To enable access to the Linear MCP server from v0, open your v0 settings and connect your Linear workspace here . Once connected, you can toggle on the connection from the main v0 input page.
